(CNN) -- Authorities investigating the case of a boy who disappeared in Kansas almost a decade ago plan to search an undisclosed residence Wednesday, the Butler County sheriff said. An age-progression photo shows what Adam Herrman would like today, as a 21-year-old man. Sheriff Craig Murphy would not disclose details about the residence or why authorities want to search it. He said his department will also search on an area of the Whitewater River, in southern Kansas, on Saturday near where Adam Herrman was last seen. Adam was 11 when he went missing in 1999. He was living in a mobile home park in Towanda, a town about 25 miles northeast of Wichita, with his adoptive parents, Doug and Valerie Herrman, authorities said. Wichita attorney Warner Eisenbise, who is representing Adam's adoptive parents, said the couple believed Adam had run away and didn't report him missing. They "really rue the fact that they didn't" report him missing, he said Monday. A few weeks ago, an undisclosed person contacted the Wichita-Sedgwick County Exploited and Missing Child Unit, expressing concern about Adam, the sheriff said. The Herrmans told Eisenbise that Adam ran away frequently, the attorney said, and they believed he was either with his biological parents or homeless. Although the Herrmans did not report him missing, "they were very worried about him," Eisenbise said. In an interview published Tuesday in The Wichita Eagle, Valerie Herrman said Adam ran away in May 1999 after she spanked him with a belt. She said she was upset but doesn't remember why, The Eagle reported. The couple never reported Adam missing, Valerie Herrman told the paper, because they feared authorities would take Adam and his siblings away because of the spanking. The couple adopted his two younger siblings as well, according to The Eagle. "We love him, and we made a terrible mistake" by not reporting him missing, Doug Herrman told The Eagle. The couple said they searched the mobile home park and other areas for two days after Adam left. "Then we came to the conclusion that the police probably have him, and they're coming to us, probably to get us in trouble," Doug Herrman told the newspaper, but the "police never came." Authorities have searched an empty lot in the Pine Ridge Mobile Home Park where the family lived. There, police found an "answer" to one of their questions, Murphy said Monday without elaborating. Eisenbise said that on December 15, authorities also searched the Herrmans' homes in Derby, outside of Wichita, and took the couple's computer, he said. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progression picture that depicts Adam as he might appear now: a young man with blue eyes and light-colored hair. Adam had been placed in the Herrmans' care when he was about 2, Murphy said Monday. He had been named Irvin Groeninger III when he was born June 8, 1987, Murphy said, and it was not clear when his name was changed. His biological parents relinquished their rights as parents about two decades ago, and Adam and his siblings were put in foster homes, CNN affiliate KWCH reported. "I thought what I was doing for them was in the best interest of the children, and evidently it wasn't," Irvin Groeninger, Adam's biological father,  told KWCH. "If he was still in my custody, this would have never happened." Adam's sister, Tiffany Broadfoot, 22, said she had last seen her brother about 14 years ago at a birthday party. "He had the cutest little round face, little-bitty freckles right up here on the tip of his cheek," she told the station. CNN's Taylor Gandossy contributed to this report.

To the state of Kansas, he was a growing child whose adoptive parents faithfully collected monthly maintenance checks. To former neighbors in the small town of Towanda, he was a quiet boy who had moved away years ago. 

It was not until late 2008 that a chilling reality came to light: Adam Herrman had vanished in 1999 at the age of 11. For nine years, no one had reported him missing, no police search had been conducted, and his adoptive parents had allegedly continued to profit from his disappearance. 

The revelation in late 2008 sparked one of the most intense and unsettling missing child investigations in Kansas history, exposing systemic failures, horrific allegations of abuse, and a dark family secret that had remained buried in the Great Plains for nearly ten years.

---

### The Origins: From Irvin to Adam

The child at the center of the tragedy was born Irvin Groeninger III in 1988. After being placed in the state foster care system as an infant, he was adopted in the early 1990s by Douglas and Valerie Herrman, a couple living in a mobile home park in Towanda, Kansas, a town of roughly 1,300 people located just northeast of Wichita. His name was legally changed to Adam Herrman.

According to later statements from extended family members and former foster children who passed through the Herrman home, Adam’s life was marked by severity and isolation. Relatives would eventually tell investigators that Adam was subjected to severe physical abuse, often confined to small spaces, forced to sleep in a closet, and routinely punished far more harshly than the other children in the household.

Then, around late 1999, 11-year-old Adam disappeared. 

---

### A Decade of Deception (1999–2008)

When extended family members and neighbors asked where Adam had gone, Douglas and Valerie Herrman offered a rotating series of explanations. To some, they claimed the state had taken Adam back. To others, they said he had been sent to a special facility for troubled youth, or that he had been returned to his biological relatives. On occasion, they simply claimed he had thrown a tantrum and run away.

Because the Herrmans frequently moved and isolated themselves from extended family, no one pushed back against these explanations for years.

Crucially, the system failed to catch the disappearance. The Kansas Department of Social and Rehabilitation Services (SRS) continued to send the Herrmans an adoption assistance stipend of approximately $700 per month. The state paid the subsidy continuously until 2006, when Adam would have turned 18, totaling tens of thousands of dollars paid for a child who was no longer in the home.

---

### The 2008 Breakthrough: Silence Broken

The wall of silence finally shattered in November 2008. 

Spurred by years of lingering suspicion and unresolved guilt, a relative of the Herrman family placed an anonymous tip to the Kansas SRS, revealing that Adam had not been seen since 1999. The SRS quickly passed the information to the Butler County Sheriff’s Office.

When Sheriff’s deputies reviewed their records, they were stunned: there was no record of Adam Herrman ever being reported missing, runaway, or abducted by any law enforcement agency in the country.

In December 2008, the Butler County Sheriff’s Office officially opened a missing person case and made a public plea for information, shocking the local community and making national headlines.

"How does an 11-year-old child vanish off the face of the Earth for ten years and nobody says a word?" Butler County Sheriff Craig Murphy asked reporters during a December 2008 press conference. "That is the question we are trying to answer."

---

### The 2008 Investigation: Digging for Answers

As December 2008 progressed, the investigation rapidly escalated from a missing persons case to a homicide inquiry. 

**Conflicting Accounts:**
When initial investigators questioned Douglas and Valerie Herrman in late 2008, the couple maintained that Adam had run away in 1999 following a spanking. They claimed they did not report him missing because they were afraid the state would take their other children away. However, investigators noted glaring inconsistencies in their timelines and story. Shortly after the initial interviews, the Herrmans retained legal counsel and ceased cooperating with law enforcement.

**Searches at the Mobile Home Park:**
In mid-December 2008, law enforcement turned their attention to the Pine Ridge Mobile Home Park in Towanda, where the family lived when Adam vanished. Equipped with search warrants, Butler County deputies, Kansas Bureau of Investigation (KBI) agents, and FBI forensic teams descended on the site. 

Investigators utilized ground-penetrating radar, heavy excavation equipment, and specialized cadaver dogs to search the plot of land where the Herrmans' trailer had once stood, as well as nearby wooded areas and the banks of the Whitewater River. 

Despite days of intensive digging and sifting through soil, the 2008 searches failed to yield human remains.

---

### The Aftermath of 2008

As 2008 came to a close, the case of Adam Herrman left a profound scar on the community and raised urgent questions about oversight within adoptive support programs. 

While law enforcement lacked the physical evidence in late 2008 to immediately file murder charges, prosecutor offices in Butler County began preparing cases centered on financial fraud, child abuse, and obstruction. Investigators publically stated that they did not believe Adam was alive, framing the investigation around finding his body and bringing those responsible to justice.

The year 2008 marked the moment Adam Herrman was brought back into the light—no longer an invisible boy forgotten by the state, but a victim whose mysterious vanishing finally demanded an accounting.

*(Note: In the years following 2008, Doug and Valerie Herrman were eventually convicted in 2010 of felony theft for unlawfully continuing to accept state adoption subsidy payments for Adam after his 1999 disappearance. Despite extensive searches in subsequent years, Adam Herrman's physical remains have never been recovered, and no one has ever been charged directly in connection with his death.)*

Investigators in rural Butler County, Kansas, are preparing to launch a renewed, targeted search near the banks of the Whitewater River, marking a critical new phase in one of the most agonizing cold cases in recent Midwest history: the disappearance of Adam Herrman. 

Adam vanished in late 1999 at the age of 11. Yet, inexplicably, his disappearance was not reported to law enforcement for nearly a decade. Today, a convergence of new forensic technology, a newly released age-progression image, and intensified police focus on terrain near the boy’s former home has brought this tragic mystery back into the national spotlight.

Here is the latest on where the investigation stands.

---

### The Whitewater River Searches

According to the Butler County Sheriff’s Office, law enforcement teams—equipped with ground-penetrating radar, cadaver dog units, and heavy excavation machinery—are slated to focus their efforts on several specific plots of land adjacent to the Whitewater River, just outside Towanda. 

The area is just a short distance from the mobile home park where Adam lived with his adoptive parents, Valerie and Doug Herrman, at the time he went missing.

Sheriff’s deputies tell CNN that while the river area has been searched in fragments over the years, recent analytical reviews of historical land use, combined with tips that have trickled in since the case gained national attention, have narrowed their focus to specific, previously undisturbed embankments. 

"We are leaving no stone unturned," a lead investigator told CNN. "Whether we are searching for answers to bring a living man home or searching for a crime scene, the Whitewater River area remains central to understanding what happened to Adam in 1999."

---

### A Face for a Forgotten Boy: The NCMEC Photo

While search crews prepare to probe the muddy banks of the Whitewater, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) has released a striking new age-progressed photograph. 

The image depicts what Adam Herrman might look like today as a grown man in his late 20s. Forensic artists painstakingly blended childhood photographs of Adam with facial features of his biological family members to recreate his potential adult appearance—showing a young man with light brown hair, sharp hazel eyes, and a slight structure to his jaw.

"Age-progression images are often our most powerful tool when dealing with long-term missing children," said an NCMEC spokesperson. "Adam was erased from public view for nine years before anyone called the police. This photo is designed to put his face back in front of the world. Someone, somewhere, might recognize him."

Authorities emphasize that while the physical search near the river reflects a tragic possibility, the release of the NCMEC photo underscores that the case remains an active missing person investigation until definitive physical evidence proves otherwise.

---

### The Parents Speak: Valerie and Doug Herrman Defend Their Actions

The darkest shadow over this case remains the decade-long silence of Adam’s adoptive parents, Valerie and Doug Herrman. 

Adam disappeared around Thanksgiving in 1999. However, police were only notified in late 2008, after an estranged relative called a child abuse hotline to report that no one had seen the boy in years. During those missing years, the Herrmans continued to collect state adoption subsidy checks for Adam, totaling tens of thousands of dollars—a fact that later led to criminal financial fraud convictions for the couple.

In past interviews and statements provided through their legal representation, Valerie and Doug Herrman have maintained their innocence regarding any physical harm to Adam, offering explanations for why they never called the police.

According to Valerie Herrman, Adam was a troubled child who had repeatedly attempted to run away. She claimed that on the day he vanished, he simply walked off after being disciplined.

"He was a runner. He had run away before, and he always said he’d go find his real mother," Valerie Herrman told reporters in an earlier statement explaining their failure to report him missing. "We looked for him ourselves. We went driving around, looking for him at local hangouts. We were terrified that if we called the police, the state would step in and take our other children away from us, thinking we were unfit parents."

Doug Herrman echoed his wife’s rationale, addressing why the couple continued to accept state adoption checks for a child who was no longer in their home.

"In our minds, we believed he was alive and that he would come back," Doug Herrman stated during legal proceedings regarding the financial charges. "We thought the money would be needed for him when he returned, or to pay for things related to him. Was it a mistake not to report it? Yes. But we did not hurt our son."

Despite the parents' claims that Adam ran away, law enforcement officials remain openly skeptical. Investigators point out that an 11-year-old boy running away without shoes, money, or winter clothing—and never contacting a single friend, relative, or school official again—defies logic.

### The Road Ahead

As search teams prepare to deploy near the Whitewater River, community members in Towanda are watching closely. For nine years, Adam Herrman was a forgotten child. Now, investigators are determined to ensure he is not a forgotten victim.
